title: The Resistant Middle: Leading Change When Staff Don't Want It
learningObjectives: Understand sources of resistance to change
Distinguish between different types of resistance (fear, loss of status, genuine concerns)
Practice change leadership beyond just announcing change
Learn to build change champions vs fighting resisters
Navigate change when you can't force compliance
Develop strategies for cultural transformation, not just process change

context.yourRole: Director of Digital Government Services at Malawi's Department of E-Government. Implementing new government portal requiring all ministries to digitize their services.
context.situation: The portal is built. Policy directive issued. But staff across ministries are resisting - still using paper forms, ignoring digital system.
context.pressure: Cabinet expects results. Citizens are complaining. But you can't fire resistant staff. Need to change hearts and minds, not just policies.
context.reality: Technical change is easy. Cultural change is hard. You're learning this the hard way.

rounds.situation:
The government services portal launched 3 months ago. Policy directive: All ministries must offer services digitally. Forms digitized, training provided, portal working.

But adoption is dismal:
- Ministry of Health: 12% of permit applications digital, 88% still paper
- Ministry of Lands: 5% of land registration digital
- Ministry of Business: 15% of business licensing digital

You visit Health Ministry to understand why:

You (to Health IT Coordinator): 'Why is digital adoption so low? Portal is working, staff are trained.'

IT Coordinator (Joseph): 'Working technically, yes. But staff won't use it.'

You: 'Why not?'

Joseph: 'Come, I'll show you.'

He takes you to permit processing office. You observe:

Staff member (Grace, 55 years old) manually processing paper permit application. There's a computer on her desk, unused.

You (to Grace): 'Good morning. Why aren't you using the digital portal for this application?'

Grace (defensive): 'I don't know how to use it properly. I went to training, but I'm not good with computers. Paper is what I know.'

You: 'But training was provided. You know the steps.'

Grace: 'The training was too fast. Young people understand computers. I'm old. I'll make mistakes on computer. Paper, I don't make mistakes.'

You notice: Fear of technology, fear of looking incompetent.

Another staff member (Patrick, 40s):

You: 'Patrick, do you use the portal?'

Patrick: 'Sometimes. But the paper system works fine. Digital creates more work - I have to enter data twice (citizens' paper forms AND into computer). With paper, I just process the form. Why add extra work?'

You: 'Citizens could apply online directly, then you wouldn't need to re-enter.'

Patrick: 'But citizens don't apply online. They come with paper. So I'm stuck re-entering. It's inefficient.'

He has a point. Citizens haven't shifted to digital applications, so staff are doing double entry.

Senior officer (Dr. Banda, department head):

You: 'Dr. Banda, you're head of department. Can you direct staff to use portal?'

Dr. Banda: 'I've told them. But I'm also busy. I don't have time to police whether they use computer or paper. As long as permits get processed, I don't care how.'

You: 'But the directive says digital.'

Dr. Banda: 'Directives are easy to issue, hard to enforce. My staff are overworked. If they prefer paper, I won't force them. It's not my priority.'

You're seeing multiple forms of resistance:
- **Fear-based** (Grace: afraid of technology, looking incompetent)
- **Rational** (Patrick: digital creates more work with current citizen behavior)
- **Indifference** (Dr. Banda: has other priorities, won't enforce)

Back at your office, your Deputy (Stella):

Stella: 'What did you find at Health?'

You: 'Resistance. Fear, rational concerns, unsupportive management. We assumed building the portal and issuing directive would work. We didn't think about change management.'

Stella: 'So what do we do? We can't fire everyone who won't use it.'
rounds.prompt: You're facing multi-layered resistance to digital transformation. What's your change strategy?
evaluationCriteria: **Resistance Types**: Do they distinguish between fear-based, rational, and indifference-based resistance?
**Different Strategies**: Do they recognize each type needs different response?
**Champions vs Resisters**: Do they think about building momentum with willing adopters vs fighting unwilling?
**Systemic Issues**: Do they identify systemic problems (citizens still use paper, so double entry)?
**Empathy**: Do they show empathy for Grace's fear vs dismissing it?
**Long-term View**: Do they accept this is culture change, takes time, can't be forced?
rounds.coachingNotes: Classic change resistance. You built system (technical), issued directive (policy), but didn't address human factors. Grace's fear is real - she's 55, not computer-literate, afraid of looking incompetent. Patrick's concern is rational - digital does create double work when citizens still bring paper. Dr. Banda's indifference - he's busy, this isn't his priority. Different resistances need different responses: [1] Grace (fear) → Patient one-on-one support, peer mentoring, celebrating small wins, [2] Patrick (rational) → Fix the systemic issue (get citizens to apply online, remove double work), [3] Dr. Banda (indifference) → Make it his priority (tie to performance metrics, show benefits to his department). You can't force change. You need to: [1] Build champions (find early adopters), [2] Address systemic issues (why is digital harder than paper?), [3] Support fearful staff (not punish), [4] Align incentives (make leaders care). This is change management.

rounds.situation:
You develop change strategy:

**STRATEGY 1: Build Champions (Not Fight Resisters)**

You identify early adopters across ministries - younger staff comfortable with technology.

You: 'I'm looking for Digital Champions in each ministry. People who believe in digital services and can help colleagues. You'd get: recognition, training on advanced features, quarterly networking with other champions. Interested?'

12 staff volunteer across 6 ministries. All younger, tech-comfortable.

You train them as peer supporters. Their job: Help colleagues use portal, celebrate wins, provide gentle encouragement.

At Health Ministry, Digital Champion (Jane) works with Grace:

Jane (gently): 'Grace, I'll help you. Let's do one permit together on the portal. I'll sit with you, guide you. No pressure.'

Grace (hesitant): 'I'll be slow...'

Jane: 'That's fine. We're learning.'

They process one permit digitally. Grace makes it work. Small win.

Jane: 'You did it! See, you can do this.'

Grace (small smile): 'It's not so hard when someone helps.'

Over 2 weeks, Jane sits with Grace daily. Grace's confidence builds. She's now processing 30% of permits digitally.

This is working better than you criticizing Grace.

**STRATEGY 2: Address Systemic Issues**

Patrick was right - double entry is real problem. Citizens bring paper, staff re-enter digitally. Inefficient.

You launch citizen awareness campaign: 'Apply online at eservices.gov.mw - faster, no travel to government office.'

But weak response. Citizens don't trust online applications.

You realize: Need demonstration effect.

You work with Business Ministry (15% digital adoption - highest so far):

You: 'Let's make online applications dramatically faster. Online business license: approved in 3 days. Paper application: 3 weeks. Create speed incentive.'

Business Ministry: 'We can do that. Online is easier to track, route digitally. Paper gets stuck in mail.'

Word spreads: Online business licenses are FAST. Paper is SLOW.

Businesses start applying online. Within a month, Business Ministry digital adoption: 15% → 45%.

Now staff like Patrick see benefit - online applications are easier to process (no re-entry), faster, citizens happier.

Patrick (at Health, sees this): 'If we could make online health permits faster like Business did, citizens would apply online, I wouldn't have to re-enter.'

You: 'Want to try that?'

Patrick: 'Yes. Let's promise 5-day approval for online, 15 days for paper.'

Health Ministry implements this. Within weeks, digital adoption: 12% → 35%.

You addressed Patrick's rational resistance by fixing systemic problem.

**STRATEGY 3: Make Leaders Care**

Dr. Banda (department head) was indifferent. You need him to care.

You work with Cabinet Office to tie digital adoption to department performance metrics:

Cabinet Secretary issues memo: 'Digital services adoption will be reported quarterly to Cabinet. Departments with low adoption will be asked to explain delays.'

Suddenly Dr. Banda cares. His department performance is now visible to Cabinet.

Dr. Banda (calls you): 'I need to increase our digital adoption. How can I help?'

You: 'Support your Digital Champion (Jane). Recognize staff who adopt digital. Monitor adoption weekly. Show leadership.'

Dr. Banda starts attending weekly check-ins, praising staff who use portal. Adoption accelerates.

But then, a setback:

**The Portal Crashes**

Wednesday 10 AM: Portal down for 4 hours.

Staff reactions:

Grace: 'See? I knew computers aren't reliable. Paper never crashes. I'm going back to paper.'

Patrick: 'This is embarrassing. We told citizens online is faster. Now it's down. We look incompetent.'

Dr. Banda: 'This undermines everything we've been building. Staff trust was fragile. One crash and they'll abandon digital.'

You realize: Technical reliability is part of change management. One failure can undo weeks of confidence-building.
rounds.prompt: Your change strategies were working. Then portal crashed. How do you prevent this from derailing adoption?
evaluationCriteria: **Crisis Response**: Do they respond to the crash quickly and transparently?
**Trust Repair**: Do they think about rebuilding trust that was damaged?
**Learning from Failure**: Do they frame crash as learning opportunity, not disaster?
**Prevention**: Do they address technical reliability to prevent future crashes?
**Resilience Building**: Do they help champions (Jane, Patrick, Dr. Banda) stay committed despite setback?
**Honesty**: Do they acknowledge the problem vs downplaying?
rounds.coachingNotes: The crash is a critical moment. You've been building trust slowly (Grace learning with Jane, Patrick seeing benefits, Dr. Banda supporting). One crash can destroy that trust. Your response: [1] **Immediate**: Fix the crash ASAP, communicate transparently about cause and timeline. [2] **Acknowledge**: 'Yes, this is frustrating. We're sorry. Here's what happened and what we're doing to prevent it.' Don't minimize or make excuses. [3] **Support champions**: Call Jane, Patrick, Dr. Banda personally. They've been advocating for digital - crash makes them look bad. Reassure them, explain fix, ask them to stay committed. [4] **Prevent**: Invest in redundancy, monitoring, faster incident response. Technical reliability is prerequisite for adoption. [5] **Frame**: 'Every system has issues. What matters is how we respond. We're learning and improving.' The change management lesson: Trust is built slowly, destroyed quickly. Technical failures in change process are particularly damaging because resisters seize on them ('I told you so'). Must respond impeccably.

rounds.situation:
You respond to the crash:

**Immediate Communication:**
You send message to all Digital Champions and Department Heads within 30 minutes:

'Portal experienced outage due to database issue. Fixed within 4 hours. Cause: query optimization failure. Prevention: We're implementing database monitoring and redundant failover. Apologies for disruption.'

**Personal Calls:**
You call Jane, Patrick, Dr. Banda:

You (to Jane): 'I know the crash was frustrating, especially as you've been building Grace's confidence. I'm sorry. Here's what we're doing to prevent this: [technical fixes]. Please reassure Grace this was one-time issue, not systemic unreliability.'

Jane: 'Grace was saying "I knew it" when it crashed. I'll talk to her. But you need to make sure this doesn't happen again. My credibility is on the line.'

You: 'I understand. We're taking reliability seriously.'

**Town Hall:**
You hold virtual town hall with all staff using portal:

You: 'I want to address Wednesday's outage. It was unacceptable. You're adopting digital services, trusting the system, and it let you down. Here's what happened [technical explanation]. Here's what we're doing: [1] Redundant database servers so one failure doesn't crash system, [2] 24/7 monitoring to catch issues faster, [3] Backup plan for staff if portal is down. We're learning and improving. Thank you for your patience.'

Q&A:

Staff: 'What should we do if portal goes down again? We can't just stop serving citizens.'

You: 'Good question. We're developing: [1] Paper backup forms that can be entered into system later, [2] Portal status page so you know if it's down or your internet, [3] Support hotline for technical issues. You'll never be stuck.'

This reassures staff.

**Six months after launch:**

Digital adoption across ministries:
- Health: 62% (Grace is now Digital Champion herself, helping other older staff)
- Business: 78% (nearly all online due to speed advantage)
- Lands: 45% (improving, but complex land records hard to digitize)
- Average across government: 52%

You've learned:

**What Worked:**
1. **Digital Champions** - Peer support more effective than top-down mandates
2. **Addressing rational resistance** - Made online faster, removed double work
3. **Leadership engagement** - When Dr. Banda cared, adoption accelerated
4. **Celebrating wins** - Recognizing staff who adopted digital
5. **Fixing systemic issues** - Citizen awareness, speed incentives

**What Didn't Work:**
1. **Initial approach** - Assuming directive + training = adoption
2. **Ignoring fear** - Grace's anxiety was real, needed empathy
3. **One-time training** - Needed ongoing support

**Still Struggling:**
1. **Hardcore resisters** - 5-10% of staff won't adopt no matter what
2. **Complex services** - Land registration is hard to digitize
3. **Rural areas** - Internet connectivity limits digital services

**Your Reflection:**

Stella: 'What's your biggest learning from this change effort?'

You: 'Change is not: Build → Announce → Train → Mandate. Change is: Build → Pilot → Learn → Adapt → Support → Iterate → Celebrate → Scale. It's messy, slow, requires empathy. We were impatient. We've learned to meet people where they are.'

Stella: 'What about the hardcore resisters? Some staff will never adopt.'

You: '80/20 rule. If we get 80% adoption, that's success. Chasing the last 20% is exhausting. Focus energy on willing adopters, not fighting unwilling. Eventually, social norm shifts - digital becomes the default, paper becomes the exception. The holdouts retire or adapt when they're the only ones on paper. You can't force everyone. You build momentum with the willing, create environment where digital is easier than paper, let social pressure do the rest.'

Stella: 'So we accept some resistance?'

You: 'We accept that change is gradual. We went from 8% to 52% adoption in 6 months. That's real progress. Perfect is the enemy of good. Focus on the 52%, not the 48%. Keep improving the system, supporting staff, celebrating wins. Adoption will grow.'

**LESSONS ON CHANGE MANAGEMENT:**

1. **Change is human, not just technical** - Building system is 20% of work, changing behavior is 80%
2. **Understand resistance** - Fear (Grace), rational concerns (Patrick), indifference (Dr. Banda) need different responses
3. **Build champions, don't fight resisters** - Peer support more effective than mandates
4. **Fix systemic issues** - If digital is harder than paper, people won't adopt
5. **Make it advantageous** - Online faster than paper = people switch for self-interest
6. **Support, don't punish** - Grace needed help, not criticism
7. **Leaders matter** - When Dr. Banda cared, adoption accelerated
8. **Celebrate early wins** - Recognition motivates others
9. **Expect setbacks** - Portal crash was opportunity to show reliability commitment
10. **Accept gradual progress** - 80% adoption is success, don't exhaust yourself chasing 100%
rounds.prompt: When leading change, how do you balance being patient (people need time) vs being demanding (we need results)?
evaluationCriteria: **Both Are Important**: Do they recognize need for both patience and drive?
**Milestones**: Do they think about setting milestones (3 months, 6 months) to assess progress?
**Differentiation**: Do they treat willing adopters differently from resistant?
**Systemic vs Individual**: Do they fix systemic barriers while supporting individuals?
**Sustainable Pace**: Do they avoid burnout (yours and team's) from being too demanding?
**Results Focus**: Do they keep eye on actual adoption numbers, not just activities?
rounds.coachingNotes: Balance patience and demands: [1] **Set milestones**: 'In 3 months, we want 30% adoption. In 6 months, 50%.' This gives timeframe without being unrealistic. [2] **Differentiate**: Be patient with fearful staff (Grace - needs ongoing support). Be firmer with indifferent leaders (Dr. Banda - he has responsibility to lead). [3] **Fix systemic barriers quickly**: Don't wait months to address double-entry problem. Fast action on systems, patient with people. [4] **Celebrate progress**: 52% adoption in 6 months is real achievement. Acknowledge it, don't only focus on the 48% who haven't adopted. [5] **Sustainable pace**: Change takes time. If you burn yourself out trying to force 100% adoption in 3 months, you'll fail. Better: 80% in a year with sustainable approach. [6] **Results-focused**: Track actual adoption numbers weekly. If stuck, diagnose why and adapt. Don't confuse activities (trainings, meetings) with results (adoption). Be patient with people's learning curves, demanding on systemic barriers and measurable progress.

keyTakeaways: Change is 20% technical (building system) and 80% human (changing behavior and culture)
Resistance has different sources: fear, rational concerns, indifference - each needs different response
Building champions (peer supporters) more effective than fighting resisters
Make change advantageous (online faster than paper) so people adopt from self-interest, not just compliance
Fix systemic issues that make new way harder than old way
Support fearful staff with patient coaching, don't punish them
Engage leaders - when they care, change accelerates
Technical reliability matters - one system crash can undermine weeks of trust-building
Accept gradual progress - 80% adoption is success, perfect is enemy of good
Change is iterative - build, learn, adapt, support, celebrate, scale

frameworks.name: Resistance Diagnosis
frameworks.description: Diagnose type of resistance: [1] Fear-based (afraid of change, looking incompetent) → Response: Patient support, coaching, celebrating small wins, [2] Rational (change creates real problems) → Response: Fix systemic issues, [3] Indifference (don't care) → Response: Align incentives, make it their priority.
frameworks.application: Grace (fear) got peer mentoring. Patrick (rational) got faster online process to remove double-work. Dr. Banda (indifference) got performance metrics tied to adoption.

frameworks.name: Change Champions Network
frameworks.description: Identify early adopters in each unit. Train as peer supporters. Their role: [1] Help colleagues adopt new system, [2] Celebrate early wins, [3] Provide gentle encouragement, [4] Report barriers to leadership. Build momentum with willing, not fight unwilling.
frameworks.application: Jane (Digital Champion) worked with Grace one-on-one, built confidence. More effective than you mandating Grace use portal.

frameworks.name: Advantage Design
frameworks.description: Make new way better than old way in ways people care about: [1] Faster, [2] Easier, [3] Higher quality, [4] More status/recognition. People adopt from self-interest, not just compliance.
frameworks.application: Online business licenses: 3 days. Paper: 3 weeks. Speed advantage drove citizen adoption, which made staff adoption easier (no double-entry). Self-interest, not mandate.

frameworks.name: Change Milestones
frameworks.description: Set adoption targets with timeframes: [1] Month 3: 30% adoption, [2] Month 6: 50%, [3] Month 12: 75%. Track weekly. If stuck, diagnose barriers and adapt approach. Balance: patient with people, demanding on progress.
frameworks.application: You went from 8% to 52% in 6 months. If stuck at 52%, would diagnose: What's preventing the next 25%? Fix barriers, keep progressing.

frameworks.name: Technical Reliability as Trust
frameworks.description: In change management, technical failures destroy trust faster than successes build it. When system fails: [1] Respond immediately, [2] Communicate transparently, [3] Support champions (they advocated, now look bad), [4] Fix + prevent, [5] Frame as learning, not disaster.
frameworks.application: Portal crash threatened to undermine adoption. Immediate fix, transparent communication, personal support to champions (Jane), technical improvements prevented trust collapse.
